title: Freya and the Clock
premise: In the waning years of a continental war, battlefield nurse Jonah Vasquez keeps a hidden ledger of the dead and displaced that official histories omit, believing invisibility is her only safety. When a mute child named Freya is left at the field hospital's door clutching a broken clock, Jonah is drawn into the orbit of the very officers whose omissions she has been documenting. As the armistice approaches, Jonah must choose between the quiet love of a disgraced cartographer and her duty to deliver the ledger to a war tribunal before the victors' historians can burn the record. She succeeds at devastating personal cost, publishing the truth under the child's name rather than her own, and the novel closes decades later with Freya, grown, winding the repaired clock in a museum where the ledger finally hangs.
about_author: Yara Vane is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed wartime correspondence in provincial European collections. She writes historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Ledger of Small Names
chapters.summary: Jonah Vasquez, a battlefield nurse, records in a hidden notebook the names of the dead that officers' reports omit. POV: Jonah. The beat is quiet defiance—she believes history happens elsewhere, to other people, and that her invisibility is a kind of armor.

chapters.title: A Child at the Door
chapters.summary: A mute girl is left at the field hospital's entrance at dawn, holding a shattered clock and a note: forget the face. Jonah, against orders, takes her in. POV: Jonah. Emotional beat: the first crack in Jonah's conviction that she can remain uninvolved.

chapters.title: The Cartographer's Error
chapters.summary: Disgraced cartographer Elias Brandt arrives to redraw retreat maps and recognizes the clock as a piece from a village erased from official maps. POV: Elias. Beat: two keepers of erased things recognize each other, though neither says so aloud.

chapters.title: Freya Does Not Speak
chapters.summary: Jonah tries to learn the girl's origin; Freya communicates only through arranging objects, including the clock's gears. POV: Jonah. Beat: tenderness tangled with dread—caring for Freya makes Jonah legible to the camp's suspicious commandant.

chapters.title: The Commandant's Courtesy
chapters.summary: Commandant Reiss visits the ward, charming and watchful, asking pointed questions about 'unregistered persons.' POV: Jonah. Beat: fear sharpened into resolve; Jonah hides the ledger inside the clock's casing.

chapters.title: Names in the Margin
chapters.summary: Elias discovers Jonah's ledger and confronts her: his own brother's name is in it, unrecorded anywhere else. POV: Elias. Beat: grief and gratitude collide; Elias pledges to help, asking nothing in return—yet.

chapters.title: The Village That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Elias decodes the clock's engraving, locating the erased village of Halden and Freya's likely family. POV: Elias. Beat: hope kindled, then complicated—Halden's erasure was ordered by men still in command.

chapters.title: An Officer's Debt
chapters.summary: Major Corwin, dying of wounds, confesses to Jonah that he signed the order erasing Halden and begs her to record his name beside it. POV: Jonah. Beat: the moral weight of witness—she writes it down, hating that she must.

chapters.title: What the Nurses Know
chapters.summary: The nursing staff forms a silent network to move supplies and information; Jonah realizes the ledger is not hers alone. POV: Jonah. Beat: solidarity; invisibility reframed as collective, purposeful concealment rather than cowardice.

chapters.title: Reiss Closes the Net
chapters.summary: Reiss institutes inspections and announces that 'unregistered children' will be transferred after the armistice. POV: Jonah. Beat: the clock starts ticking—Freya will be disappeared like her village.

chapters.title: The Armistice Rumor
chapters.summary: News of imminent armistice splits the camp: some celebrate, others begin burning documents. POV: Elias. Beat: urgency—Elias learns historians attached to the victors are already compiling the official record, omissions included.

chapters.title: A Map With Two Truths
chapters.summary: Elias draws a false route for Reiss while secretly mapping Halden's true location for the tribunal. POV: Elias. Beat: love declared obliquely—Elias tells Jonah the map is for her, and what that means.

chapters.title: The Confession Ward
chapters.summary: Wounded soldiers, believing they are dying, give Jonah their omitted names; the ledger swells past two hundred entries. POV: Jonah. Beat: the ledger transforms from protest to sacred trust, raising the cost of failure.

chapters.title: Reiss Finds the Clock
chapters.summary: An inspection nearly uncovers the ledger; Freya, in her first spoken word, lies to protect Jonah—'broken.' POV: Jonah. Beat: shattering tenderness; the child protects the woman, and Jonah can no longer pretend neutrality.

chapters.title: The Price of the Record
chapters.summary: Reiss, suspicious, arrests Elias for falsified maps. POV: Elias, in a cell. Beat: sacrifice accepted—Elias refuses to implicate Jonah, knowing the ledger matters more than his life.

chapters.title: Tribunal at the Crossroads
chapters.summary: Armistice signed; a tribunal convoy passes within a day's ride. Jonah must choose: flee with Freya to safety or carry the ledger to the historians before Reiss's men destroy it. POV: Jonah. Beat: love against duty made literal.

chapters.title: The Burning Ward
chapters.summary: Reiss orders the hospital's records burned and the ward evacuated as cover. Jonah, disguised among the wounded, smuggles the clock-ledger out under shellfire. POV: Jonah. Beat: terror transfigured into purpose; she is visible at last, and it nearly kills her.

chapters.title: Freya Speaks
chapters.summary: Cornered at a checkpoint, Freya testifies—fluently, devastatingly—naming the soldiers of Halden, her memory intact beneath her silence. POV: Freya. Beat: the climax of voice; the child the officers ordered forgotten becomes the record's chief witness.

chapters.title: What the Historians Kept
chapters.summary: Jonah delivers the ledger to the tribunal, but the victors' historians offer to publish only a sanitized version crediting an officer. POV: Jonah. Beat: bitter triumph—truth survives, but authorship is a battlefield too.

chapters.title: Reckoning at Halden
chapters.summary: The tribunal excavates Halden; Reiss is named in the record he tried to burn, and Elias is freed to draw the village back onto the map. POV: Elias. Beat: restoration with scars—maps, names, and the living are returned, but not whole.

chapters.title: The Name She Chose
chapters.summary: Jonah publishes the ledger under 'Freya' rather than her own name, choosing the child's witness over her own credit, and formally adopts her. POV: Jonah. Beat: resolution of the love-versus-duty thread—she learns that being seen was never the danger; being silent was.

chapters.title: The Clock, Wound
chapters.summary: Decades later, Freya—grown, a historian herself—winds the repaired clock in a museum where the ledger hangs, Jonah's final page pinned beside it. POV: Freya. Beat: inheritance completed; memory, once contraband, becomes the thing we hand to the future.
